The classical antiepileptics may not be particularly effec- tive for atonic or tonic seizures, which are often associat- ed with specific epileptic syndromes or with cerebral dam- age or mental retardation. UK guidelines suggest valproate or lamotrigine as first-line drugs; clobazam, clonazepam, levetiracetam, or topiramate are possible second-line drugs, and others that have been tried include acetazolamide and the barbiturates such as phenobarbital, while phenytoin may be considered for tonic seizures.16 In catamenial epilepsy (epilepsy associated with men- struation) seizures can be predicted and intermittent thera- py with clobazam may be useful. Hormonal manipulation has also been tried using progestogens, gonadorelin ana- logues, and clomifene.42 The Lennox-Gastaut syndrome begins in early child- hood and is particularly difficult to treat because multiple seizure types co-exist; seizures rarely remit entirely. Val- proate is most frequently used43 because of its broad spec- trum of activity; UK guidelines consider lamotrigine or topiramate as alternative first-line drugs if valproate is unsuitable; second-line choices include clobazam, clon- azepam, ethosuximide, or levetiracetam.16 Felbamate has also been used. The optimum treatment remains uncertain, but monotherapy with any drug has not been shown to be particularly effective.44 The classical antiepileptics are often ineffective in infan- tile spasms (as for example in West’s syndrome).45 UK guidelines recommend treatment with corticotropin or a corticosteroid, or else with vigabatrin;16 in the USA, how- ever, the American Academy of Neurology considers that the evidence does not support the use of corticosteroids, although corticotropin or vigabatrin appear to be of bene- fit.46 Vigabatrin is effective either as adjunctive treatment or monotherapy. Many consider that, despite the risk of visual field defects,47 it should replace corticotropin or cor- ticosteroids as the treatment of choice,48-54 although others disagree.55,56 However, vigabatrin may offer the best first option in the treatment of infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis.54,57,58 In some countries, valproate, alone or with clonazepam and/or pyridoxine, has been tried for initial management of infantile spasms.59 Other second-line drugs include clobazam and topiramate;16 nitrazepam,16,48 felbamate,45,60 and lamotrigine45,60 have also been used.
